Mount Everest is the world's highest mountain at twenty-nine thousand thirty-two feet, located in the Himalayas on the Nepal-Tibet border. Above twenty-six thousand feet lies the death zone where insufficient oxygen cannot sustain human life for extended periods. Known in Nepali as Sagarmatha and in Tibetan as Chomolungma, meaning Goddess Mother of the World, the mountain remains the supreme test of mountaineering skill, endurance, and determination. Edmund Hillary and Sherpa Tenzing Norgay made the first successful ascent in nineteen fifty-three as part of a British expedition led by John Hunt, an achievement that captured the world's imagination. Hundreds of climbers attempt the peak each year during the brief spring weather window in May. Over three hundred people have died on the mountain since records began. The primary routes are the South Col route from Nepal, which is more frequently climbed, and the North Col route from Tibet. Avalanches, falling ice, extreme cold, and altitude sickness are the principal killers, and many bodies remain on the mountain. The Sherpas, indigenous to the region, provide essential climbing support and have become synonymous with high-altitude mountaineering.
